sermon:
## No Other Gospel: Why Adding to Grace Is Deserting It (Galatians 1:1-24)
*Paul had no patience for a slightly improved gospel, because a slightly improved gospel is a different god*

**Text:** Galatians 1:1-24 · **Supporting:** Galatians 5:9 · Acts 15:1 · Romans 1:16-17 · 2 Corinthians 11:14 · Jeremiah 6:14 · Deuteronomy 27:26

Somewhere in the churches of Galatia, around the year 49, a message arrived that sounded like an upgrade. Not a denial of Christ. An addition to him. Believe in Jesus, yes, and also be circumcised. Trust the cross, yes, and also keep the calendar. It did not feel like a departure. It felt like maturity. It felt like taking the faith seriously. And Paul, who normally opens a letter by thanking God for the people he is writing to, opens this one with his hand already shaking.

He does not thank God. He does not warm them up. He tells them they are deserting the one who called them, and he does it in the first ten sentences. A modern reader flinches at the temperature. We have been trained to think the sign of a healthy soul is that it never gets this hot. But this is the heat of a man watching people he loves drink poison that has been relabeled as medicine, and refusing to call it anything gentler than what it is.

We live in a moment that no longer knows what to do with this letter. A post-Christian culture has kept the vocabulary of grace and lost the thing itself, and it has replaced it with a gospel of performance so total that it does not even recognize itself as religion. Be your best self. Earn your worth. Prove you belong. The Galatian heresy did not die. It secularized. And then it walked back into the church wearing our own clothes, and we welcomed it, because a gospel we can perform is a gospel we can control.

### I. A Gospel Not Invented by Men (Galatians 1:1-12)

Paul begins by establishing where his message came from, because the whole argument depends on it. If the gospel is something men worked out, then men can amend it. If it is something God revealed, then no one can. The Judaizers were treating the gospel as a working draft. Paul treats it as a verdict already handed down.

Watch the opening claim. "Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead" (Galatians 1:1). Before he defends the message he defends its source. His apostleship did not come up through a human chain of command. It came down. The Greek preposition matters here: *apo anthrōpōn*, not *from* men, and *di' anthrōpou*, not *through* man. Neither the origin nor the channel was human. This is a man refusing to let his authority be reduced to a credential someone else could revoke.

Then the sentence that should have stopped the whole crisis cold. "I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel—not that there is another one" (Galatians 1:6-7). Read that carefully. He calls it a *different* gospel and then immediately says there is no such thing. A different gospel is a contradiction in terms. There is the gospel, and there is its absence wearing the gospel's clothes. The word he uses for deserting, *metatithēmi*, is the word for a soldier defecting, a man changing sides. They thought they were adding a discipline. Paul saw a defection.

- **A. The source is revelation, not committee.** — "For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man's gospel. For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ" (Galatians 1:11-12). A gospel men authored, men can renegotiate. A gospel God gave stands outside the reach of our editing. That is the whole weight of the opening.
- **B. "Quickly" is the wound.** — It was not that they abandoned grace after decades of hardship. It was how fast the drift happened, how little pressure it took. Grace is not lost in a dramatic renunciation. It is lost in a small, reasonable-sounding addition that no one thought was a big deal at the time.

### II. Let Him Be Accursed (Galatians 1:8-24)

Now the sentence that no committee would approve. "But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed" (Galatians 1:8). *Anathema.* Devoted to destruction. And then, because we might think he spoke in the heat of the moment, he says it again in the next verse, slower and colder. "As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed" (Galatians 1:9).

He curses himself in advance. Even if *we*. Even if I, Paul, come back next year with a modified version—let me be accursed. There is no name so respected, no messenger so radiant, that the message gets a pass because of who is carrying it. Paul knew the danger. Even Satan, he writes elsewhere, "disguises himself as an angel of light" (2 Corinthians 11:14). The most dangerous false gospel does not arrive looking false. It arrives looking holier than the real one.

Behind this stands a line from Deuteronomy that Paul has already begun to hear ringing. "Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them" (Deuteronomy 27:26). The law comes with a curse for anyone who fails to keep all of it. To go back under it as your ground of acceptance is not to grab a lifeline. It is to walk voluntarily back under the sentence Christ died to lift.

Notice why Paul reaches for the strongest word he has. It is not temper. It is proportion. If the gospel is the announcement that God has done for you what you could never do for yourself, then a message that adds your doing back into the equation is not a smaller gospel—it is the opposite gospel, and it damns exactly the people it promises to save. Paul is not overreacting to a minor liturgical dispute. He is reacting exactly enough to a message that, if believed, would send its hearers to hell with the word grace still on their lips. The curse is the measure of the stakes.

- **A. A little leaven leavens the whole lump.** — Paul says it plainly later in the same letter: "A little leaven leavens the whole lump" (Galatians 5:9). You cannot add a little law to grace and keep grace. The addition does not sit quietly beside grace as a supplement. It works through the whole batch until nothing of grace is left. This is why he will not treat the false teachers as slightly-off brothers. A little is not a little.
- **B. His whole life proved the point he was making.** — Paul spends the back half of the chapter on his biography for one reason. He had been the fiercest keeper of the law alive, "extremely zealous... for the traditions of my fathers" (Galatians 1:14), and he persecuted the church for grace's sake. If law-keeping could have produced a right man, it would have produced him. It produced a man breathing threats. Then God, "who had set me apart before I was born" (Galatians 1:15), reached him with grace he had spent his life fighting.

The crisis in Galatia is not ancient history. The compromise Peter would soon make in Antioch, the demand of the men from Judea in Acts 15 who said "unless you are circumcised... you cannot be saved" (Acts 15:1)—these are not old church quarrels. They are the permanent temptation of the religious heart, and the religious heart did not die in the first century.

### III. The Gospel We Keep Renegotiating

Here is the part I cannot preach from a safe distance, because I have done exactly what Paul is condemning, and I have done it from a pulpit. I have preached grace on Sunday and then, in a hundred quiet ways, taught people that God's warmth toward them rose and fell with their performance that week. I have watched a person come back to church after a hard failure and I have felt the temptation to make them earn their way back into the room. That is a different gospel. It is the Galatian heresy in a golf shirt. We did not delete the cross. We added a footnote to it, and the footnote ate the text.

We do not usually add circumcision. We add better quiet times. We add the right political tribe. We add a personality that has its act together. We add the correct opinions on the correct issues, and slowly the message becomes: Christ died for you, and now here is the actual list. That is not a stricter version of the gospel. It is its desertion wearing a lanyard.

Church history knew this fight before we did. In 1517 Luther watched the Roman church sell indulgences—grace, priced, on an installment plan—and the whole Reformation turned on the discovery, from this very letter, that a person is justified by faith apart from works. Luther called Galatians his own epistle, the one he said he had betrothed himself to, and the reason is that he had lived the addition from the inside. He had been the monk who added and added—fasts, vigils, confessions so long his own confessor grew tired of him—and the more he added to grace the less grace he had, until a man drowning in his own additions read this letter and found the bottom of the ocean was solid ground. But do not aim that only at Rome, or only at the sixteenth century. The man who preaches free grace and then rules his home by fear, who tells his sons the cross covers everything and then withholds his approval until they perform, has printed his own indulgences. I know that man. I have been that man at my own dinner table.

And here is where the accursed sentence turns, finally, to mercy. Paul is not fencing you out. He is fencing out everything that would put you back on the treadmill God already stopped. "Jesus Christ... gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father" (Galatians 1:3-4). *Gave himself.* Not lent. Not advanced against future performance. Gave. The gospel Paul refuses to let you improve is the only one that can hold the weight of a Tuesday, because it does not rest on your Tuesday at all.

- **A. The addition always feels like devotion.** — No one adds to the gospel out of laziness. We add out of a desire to take God seriously, and that is what makes it so hard to see. The Galatians thought they were growing up. Ask whether the thing you have added to grace feels like maturity. That is precisely how it will feel.
- **B. Christ crucified is the whole ground, or there is no ground.** — If Jesus gave himself for your sins, there is nothing left for you to give for them. The moment you reach back to supply the missing piece, you have said the cross came up short. It did not come up short. It came down final.

Add to grace and lose it.

## Justified by Faith, Not Works of the Law: Paul Confronts Peter (Galatians 2:1-21)
*When the gospel was on the line at a dinner table, Paul would not stay quiet to keep the peace*

**Text:** Galatians 2:1-21 · **Supporting:** Romans 3:28 · Ephesians 2:8-9 · Philippians 3:9 · Acts 10:15 · Habakkuk 2:4 · Titus 3:5

The gospel almost died at a dinner. Not in a synagogue debate, not before a tribunal, but at a table in Antioch where Peter had been eating comfortably with Gentile Christians until the wrong men walked in. Then the chief apostle stood up and moved his chair. He did not preach a false gospel. He did not write a false letter. He just quietly changed where he sat, and that small movement threatened to unmake everything the cross had accomplished. Paul saw it and did not blink.

We tend to imagine the great threats to the church as loud ones. Persecution. Heresy shouted from a stage. But the threat in this chapter came dressed as tact. It came as a respected leader deciding that peace at the table was worth a small compromise in the truth. And Paul understood something we keep forgetting: there is a kind of peace-keeping that is a betrayal, and there is a kind of confrontation that is love with its sleeves rolled up.

This matters more, not less, in a post-Christian culture, because we have made non-confrontation itself into a virtue and called it tolerance. The one unforgivable sin of our moment is to tell someone they are wrong about something that matters to them. And a church shaped by that air will produce a thousand Peters—leaders who hold the true gospel in their statements of faith and quietly rearrange their tables to avoid the discomfort of standing for it. Paul's willingness to name a beloved man's compromise to his face is not a relic of a harsher age. It is the exact courage a conflict-avoidant church has lost and cannot survive without.

### I. The Truth of the Gospel, Preserved Under Pressure (Galatians 2:1-10)

Paul begins by describing an earlier moment in Jerusalem, and the language is that of a man who went in ready to fight. He brought Titus, an uncircumcised Greek, as a living test case. He describes the opposition as "false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery" (Galatians 2:4). Notice the words. Freedom and slavery. To add the law's requirements to the gospel is not to raise the bar. It is to change the master.

And then the sentence that shows how much was at stake. "To them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you" (Galatians 2:5). Not for an hour. Not for a moment. Because the moment you concede the point once, to keep the peace, you have conceded it forever. The men who ran the church in Jerusalem—James, Cephas, John, "those who seemed to be pillars" (Galatians 2:9)—added nothing to Paul's message. They shook his hand. The gospel Paul preached to the Gentiles was not a lesser version cleared by headquarters. It was the same gospel, and headquarters knew it.

- **A. Freedom is what the false brothers came to steal.** — They did not come to add a nice discipline. They came, Paul says, to spy out freedom and manufacture slavery. Every addition to grace is a theft of freedom disguised as an offer of seriousness. The heart drawn to law-keeping should hear this: the yoke being offered is not maturity. It is a return to bondage.
- **B. The one thing they asked was to remember the poor.** — The pillars added no doctrine, but they did ask Paul to "remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do" (Galatians 2:10). Grace does not float free of the ground. The gospel that asks nothing of your performance for acceptance produces, at once, a hand open to the poor. Faith alone is never faith that stays alone.

### II. Opposed to His Face (Galatians 2:11-21)

Then Antioch. "But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned" (Galatians 2:11). Cephas is Peter. The man who walked on water, who preached at Pentecost, who had already been shown by God himself, on a rooftop in Joppa, that "what God has made clean, do not call common" (Acts 10:15). This Peter, of all people, "drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party" (Galatians 2:12). And his example was contagious. "The rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray" (Galatians 2:13). One man's cowardice at one table, and the whole room bent.

Paul's charge is precise. Peter was not "in step with the truth of the gospel" (Galatians 2:14). He did not accuse Peter of bad theology on paper. Peter's theology was fine. His feet had walked away from it. And that is the terror of this passage—that a man can hold the true gospel in his head and deny it with his chair. Orthodoxy in the mind and desertion in the body.

Out of this confrontation comes the sentence that is the spine of the whole letter and half the New Testament. "We know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ... because by works of the law no one will be justified" (Galatians 2:16). The verb is *dikaioō*—to be declared righteous, a courtroom word, a judge's gavel. Not made incrementally better. Declared right, now, on the basis of another's finished work. Paul says it three ways in one verse because he will not let it be missed. Not by works. Through faith. No one, ever, by works.

Hold the courtroom image, because it is the difference between two entire religions. In one, God's declaration comes at the end—a verdict earned across a lifetime of performance, uncertain until the last day, hanging on whether you finally did enough. In the other, the verdict comes at the beginning, spoken over you the moment you believe, on the ground of Christ's obedience and not your own. Paul is preaching the second, and Peter's chair was preaching the first. That is why a small movement at a dinner table was worth a public rebuke. The chair was announcing a verdict Peter had no right to revise—that Gentile believers were second-class until they performed—and Paul would not let the false verdict stand for the length of one meal.

- **A. Hypocrisy is doctrine you can walk away from.** — Peter did not recant a word. He moved his body. The gospel is not only something you confess with your mouth; it is something you can deny with your habits, your table, the people you will and will not be seen with. A church can affirm justification by faith in its statement of belief and deny it in who gets to sit down and eat.
- **B. If righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing.** — Here is the verdict Paul drives to. "I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose" (Galatians 2:21). This is the sharpest edge in the letter. To rebuild law-keeping as the ground of acceptance is to say the cross was unnecessary. It is to look at Golgotha and call it excessive. That is what a small compromise at a dinner table actually says.

### III. The Table We Still Rearrange

I have moved my chair. Not at a communion table—in the thousand quieter ways a pastor decides who is really acceptable. I have been warmer to the family that had its act together than to the one that came in broken and stayed broken. I have caught myself measuring people by whether they performed the culture of the church well, and calling that discernment. Peter's sin was not exotic. It was the ordinary religious instinct to be seen with the right people, and I have it in me, and so do you.

The circumcision party is always with us. It changes its badge. Today it might be the right voting record, the right vocabulary, the right posture on the right issue, the right kind of family. And we drift, the way Peter drifted, not by writing a false creed but by slowly making our fellowship narrower than the cross. When the gospel says a person is justified by faith and our table says a person is justified by belonging to our tribe, we have become the men from James, and we did not even notice we moved.

In 1934, as the German church bent its knee to the Reich and rewrote its fellowship around blood and nation, a group of pastors met at Barmen and declared that Jesus Christ, not any other lord, is the one Word of God the church must obey. It cost them. Bonhoeffer, who helped hold that line, later wrote about cheap grace—grace as a doctrine you affirm while your life walks the other way, forgiveness without repentance, the cross printed on the letterhead and denied at the door. That is exactly Peter at Antioch. The right words, the wrong table. And the answer then was the answer Paul gave: someone has to be willing to say, to a face everyone respects, that this is not in step with the truth.

And here is the mercy under the confrontation. Paul does not oppose Peter to win. He opposes him to hand him back the freedom Peter was throwing away. Listen to where it lands. "I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me" (Galatians 2:20). *Loved me. Gave himself for me.* The old performing self is dead. There is no chair left to defend, because the man who used to need a good seat at the table has been crucified. What lives now is Christ, and Christ does not measure you.

- **A. Confrontation can be the deepest form of love.** — Paul risked the friendship to save the gospel and to save Peter. There is a silence that pretends to be kindness and is actually cowardice. The friend who lets you keep drinking the poison because he does not want the awkwardness of the conversation does not love you more than Paul loved Peter. He loves you less.
- **B. The crucified self has nothing left to earn.** — If you died with Christ, then the whole economy of performing for acceptance is over. You cannot earn what has already been given to a dead man raised. The freedom is not that you now try harder. The freedom is that the one who kept score has been buried, and the one who loved you and gave himself for you has taken his place.

If law could save, Christ died needlessly.

## Abraham's Blessing and the Curse the Law Could Not Lift (Galatians 3:1-29)
*Righteousness was credited by faith centuries before the law arrived, and Christ took the curse the law could only pronounce*

**Text:** Galatians 3:1-29 · **Supporting:** Genesis 15:6 · Romans 4:3 · Habakkuk 2:4 · Deuteronomy 21:23 · Deuteronomy 27:26 · Romans 8:3-4

Paul opens this chapter not with an argument but with a name. "O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you?" (Galatians 3:1). *Bewitched*—as if a spell had been cast, as if reasonable people had been talked out of their senses. And the question he asks next is the question that dismantles every performance religion ever built. "Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?" (Galatians 3:2). You know the answer. You were there. The Spirit came when you believed, not when you performed. So why, having begun by grace, would you finish by sweat?

We do this constantly. We are saved by grace and then we set about being sanctified by anxiety. We come in through the open door of the cross and then try to stay in by climbing a wall we built ourselves. Paul's whole argument in this chapter is that the God who justified Abraham by faith two thousand years before Sinai has not switched systems on us. The gospel is older than the law, and the older thing was always grace.

### I. Counted Righteous Before the Law Existed (Galatians 3:1-18)

Paul reaches back past Moses to Abraham, and the move is devastating in its simplicity. "Just as Abraham 'believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness'" (Galatians 3:6). He is quoting Genesis 15:6, a verse spoken to Abraham 430 years before the law was given at Sinai. Abraham had no law to keep. He had a promise to believe. And when he believed it, God credited righteousness to his account. The word *counted*, *logizomai*, is a bookkeeper's word—an entry made, a balance declared. Abraham's righteousness was reckoned, not achieved.

This is the hinge. If the father of the faithful was justified by believing God before a single commandment was written, then justification never depended on the commandments. The law came later, and it came for a different reason. "Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham" (Galatians 3:7). Not those of blood. Not those of works. Those of faith. The true children of Abraham are everyone, Jew or Gentile, who does what Abraham did—takes God at his word.

Paul then presses the law's own testimony against the law-keepers. The prophet Habakkuk, standing in the ruins of a collapsing nation, had already written the sentence: "The righteous shall live by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:4). And against it stands the law's own curse: "Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them" (Galatians 3:10, quoting Deuteronomy 27:26). Read those two together and the trap closes. The law demands perfect, total, unbroken obedience—*all things*—and pronounces a curse on anyone who fails at a single point. The law was never a ladder to climb. It was a mirror that showed you the ladder was already broken.

This is the piece the Judaizers could not see and the moralist still cannot. They read the law as a menu of achievable requirements and imagined they were mostly getting them right. But the law does not grade on a curve. It says *all things*, and the smallest failure at a single point puts a man under the whole curse. So the law's real work is not to hand you a passing grade. It is to close every exit, to strip away the illusion that you were nearly there, to leave you standing with no defense at all—which is the only posture from which a person ever reaches out for grace. The law was given, in part, to make you desperate enough to stop trusting it.

- **A. The promise came first, and a promise cannot be annulled.** — "The law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void" (Galatians 3:17). A promise made and sealed cannot be canceled by a rule added centuries later. Grace has seniority. The performance system is the late arrival, and it never had the authority to overturn the promise.
- **B. The law was never meant to justify—it was meant to expose.** — "Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions" (Galatians 3:19). The law was not given to make you righteous. It was given to make you honest—to show you the gap, to shut every mouth, to make it impossible to keep pretending you had it handled. The law is a good diagnosis and a fatal cure.

### II. Christ Became a Curse for Us (Galatians 3:13-29)

Which leaves us cursed and cannot save ourselves, and into that dead end comes the sentence at the center of the chapter. "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, 'Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree'" (Galatians 3:13). Paul is quoting Deuteronomy 21:23, an ancient statute declaring a man hung on a tree to be under God's curse. The cross was a tree. Golgotha was the law's own curse, spoken over the one man who never broke it, so that it would never again be spoken over us.

The word *redeemed*, *exagorazō*, is a market word—to buy out, to purchase a slave off the block and set him free. The curse we earned was placed on the head of one who earned none of it. He did not lift the curse from a distance, wave it away, pronounce it null. He stepped under it. He became it. "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin"—Paul writes elsewhere the same shape of thing—so that the blessing promised to Abraham "might come to the Gentiles" (Galatians 3:14). The curse went one direction so the blessing could go the other.

And so the law's real function comes clear. "The law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith" (Galatians 3:24). The word is *paidagōgos*—not a teacher, but the household servant who walked a child to school and disciplined him along the way. A temporary custodian, never the destination. "But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian" (Galatians 3:25). The child has grown. The escort is dismissed. You do not go back and live your whole life under the man who was only supposed to walk you to the door.

- **A. The curse did not evaporate—it was absorbed.** — This is the offense and the glory of the cross. God did not lower the law's demand or excuse the debt. He paid it, in the body of his Son, hung on a tree under the law's own sentence. Grace is not God ignoring the curse. Grace is God taking it into himself.
- **B. In Christ the old dividing lines collapse.** — "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). The performance system runs on distinctions—who is in, who has earned it, who belongs. Faith erases the scoreboard. "And if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise" (Galatians 3:29). The inheritance comes by belonging to him, and belonging comes by faith.

### III. The Ladder We Keep Rebuilding

I have preached against works-righteousness and then gone home and lived it. I have measured my standing before God by how the sermon went, by whether the week felt disciplined, by whether I had done enough. That is Sinai smuggled back in through the pastor's own back door. I begin by the Spirit and then, when no one is watching, I try to be perfected by the flesh—and I am precisely the foolish Galatian Paul is naming. The bewitching still works. It works on the man in the pulpit as easily as the man in the pew.

We are addicted to the curse because we are addicted to control. A gospel we contribute to is a gospel we can manage. If I am justified by my performance, then at least the outcome is in my hands. Grace is harder to bear than law, because grace takes the ledger out of your hands entirely, and something in us would rather stay cursed and in control than be blessed and dependent. We keep rebuilding the ladder because we are afraid of the elevator someone else is running.

And the culture we live in only sharpens the reflex. A secular age has no cross to absorb the curse, so it has nowhere to put its guilt except back on the self, and it has built an entire economy on the exhaustion that follows. Perform your worth. Curate your image. Earn your place, daily, and prove it again tomorrow. The unbeliever and the legalist are running the same treadmill; only the branding differs. Both are still under the curse of Deuteronomy 27, trying to abide by all things and failing, and neither has heard that a man already hung on a tree and took the whole sentence down with him.

The Reformation turned on exactly this verse. Luther, an Augustinian monk tormented by a righteousness he could not produce, read in this letter that the just shall live by faith and later said he felt himself born again and to have gone through open gates into paradise. He had spent years trying to climb the ladder of the law, punishing his own body, and discovered that Christ had already stood at the bottom of it and taken the curse. That is not a sixteenth-century footnote. That is every soul that has ever tried to earn what can only be received, which is to say, that is mine.

And here is where the weight tips toward mercy. If Christ became a curse for you, there is no curse left with your name on it. The worst thing the law could say about you has already been said—over him, on a tree, once, finally. "In Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith" (Galatians 3:26). Not servants working toward sonship. Sons, now, through faith. The blessing of Abraham, the whole inheritance, comes to you not because you kept the law but because the one who kept it perfectly took the curse you earned and handed you the blessing he earned.

- **A. Faith is not a lesser work—it is the end of working.** — Do not turn faith into the one thing you finally perform well enough to be saved. Faith is not your contribution to the ledger. Faith is the empty hand that stops trying to pay and simply receives what Abraham received: a righteousness credited, not achieved.
- **B. You cannot be more accepted than you already are in Christ.** — There is no rung above the one you are standing on. If you are Christ's, you are Abraham's heir, and an heir does not climb toward the inheritance. He receives it because of whose he is. Stop building the ladder. The curse is lifted, and it was lifted at a tree.

Faith receives what works could never earn.

## Sons and Heirs, No Longer Slaves: The Fullness of Time (Galatians 4:1-31)
*God did not send his Son to make better slaves, but to make sons who call him Father*

**Text:** Galatians 4:1-31 · **Supporting:** Romans 8:15-17 · John 1:12 · Genesis 21:10 · Isaiah 54:1 · Ephesians 1:5 · Mark 14:36

There is a difference between an heir who does not yet know it and an heir who does. Paul says a child destined to inherit everything, while still a minor, "is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything" (Galatians 4:1). Same house. Same food. Same schedule under a guardian. From the outside you could not tell the heir from the servant. The difference was not in his conduct. It was in his identity, and one day that identity would break out into the open and change everything about how he lived in his father's house.

The Galatians were being talked into trading sonship for slavery and calling it devotion. They had been made heirs, and now men were persuading them to go back and live like servants working to earn a place they already owned. Paul is not disputing whether they should obey God. He is disputing on what basis they stand in the house at all—as hired hands anxious about their standing, or as sons who cannot be un-sonned.

### I. When the Fullness of Time Had Come (Galatians 4:1-11)

Paul locates the whole gospel inside a moment of history. "But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons" (Galatians 4:4-5). *The fullness of time*—God did not act at random. He waited until the exact hour, and then he moved. The Son was born under the very law that held us, stepped inside the prison to open it from within.

And the purpose clause is everything: *so that we might receive adoption as sons*. The Greek is *huiothesia*, a legal term from the Roman world—the formal, irreversible act by which a person was placed as a son with full rights of inheritance. Not taken in on trial. Not on probation. Adopted, with all the legal weight of a natural-born heir. Redemption was not the goal. It was the means. The goal was sonship.

Then Paul names the proof that it worked, and it is a sound. "Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, 'Abba! Father!'" (Galatians 4:6). *Abba*—the Aramaic word a child uses for his father, the word Jesus himself cried in Gethsemane when he said, "Abba, Father, all things are possible for you" (Mark 14:36). The Spirit puts the Son's own word for the Father into your mouth. That cry is not something you work up. It is evidence of a status already granted. "So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God" (Galatians 4:7).

- **A. Redemption was the road; sonship was the destination.** — He redeemed us *so that* we might be adopted. If you stop at forgiveness you have stopped short of the point. The debt was canceled in order that you might be placed in the family, and a man who only knows he is forgiven, but not that he is a son, is still living like a servant with a clean record.
- **B. Going back to the law is going back to slavery.** — Paul cannot believe what he is watching. "How can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?" (Galatians 4:9). The religion of performance is not a step up from immaturity. It is a return to the nursery, to the guardians and the calendar-watching, "days and months and seasons and years" (Galatians 4:10)—the anxious observance of a slave, from a son who has forgotten who he is.

### II. The Two Sons and the Two Covenants (Galatians 4:12-31)

Paul then does something tender before he does something sharp. He reminds them of how they first received him—sick, weak, unimpressive—and how they welcomed him "as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus" (Galatians 4:14), and would have torn out their own eyes for him. Now he asks, grieved rather than merely angry, "Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?" (Galatians 4:16). This is a pastor's wound, not a debater's point. The people he labored over are slipping, and the men flattering them are the ones who mean them harm.

Then the sharp thing—an allegory from Abraham's own household. Abraham had two sons. Ishmael, "born according to the flesh," to the slave woman Hagar; and Isaac, "born through promise," to the free woman Sarah (Galatians 4:23). Ishmael was the product of Abraham and Sarah trying to help God keep his promise through their own effort—the child of works. Isaac was the child God gave when human effort had run out, born to a woman past childbearing—the child of promise. Two ways of trying to get an heir. One by the flesh. One by faith.

And Paul, quoting Isaiah's promise to a barren woman, "Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear" (Galatians 4:27, from Isaiah 54:1), says the free woman is the mother of us all. Then the hard word from Genesis: "Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman" (Galatians 4:30, from Genesis 21:10). The flesh and the promise cannot share the inheritance. You cannot be half-slave and half-son. Sarah's line and Hagar's line do not merge.

- **A. Grace-people are children of promise, not products of effort.** — Isaac existed because God kept a promise, not because Abraham engineered a solution. If you belong to Christ, you are not the achievement of your own religious striving. You are the gift God gave when your effort had run dry. The child of the flesh is what you can produce. The child of promise is what only God can give.
- **B. The pastoral pain is real—truth-telling is not enmity.** — Paul's anguish, "I am in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in you" (Galatians 4:19), tells you the temperature of this letter. He is not scoring points. He is a mother in labor over people he is watching walk into bondage. The friend who tells you the hard truth has not become your enemy. He has become the only one still telling you the truth.

### III. The House We Keep Mistaking for a Workhouse

I have lived in my Father's house like a hired hand. Forgiven, adopted, an heir of everything—and I have gotten up in the morning anxious about my standing, working to earn a place that was already deeded to me. I have preached adoption and parented my own five sons, at times, as if my approval of them rose and fell with their performance—which is a lie about God that I acted out at my own kitchen table. A man who was raised without a father should know better than anyone what a Father freely giving sonship means. And still I revert to the workhouse. The slave's reflex outlives the slave's chains.

We prefer the workhouse because the workhouse keeps us in control. If my standing depends on my performance, then at least I am running the ledger, and there is a grim comfort in that. Sonship is harder to bear, because a son cannot earn his way in and cannot earn his way out—the whole thing rests on the Father, and something in us would rather be an anxious servant with a job to do than a beloved son with nothing to prove. We turn back to the elementary principles because slavery, for all its weight, at least feels like it is ours to manage.

A fatherless culture makes this worse, and ours is one. A generation raised without the settled, unearned welcome of a father learns early that love is a wage—that affection is something you perform for and can lose. It carries that lesson into every room, including the sanctuary, and it hears the word Father and braces for a boss. This is not a modern footnote to Galatians 4. It is the exact wound the chapter speaks to. Into a world full of orphans working for approval, God does not send a better set of rules. He sends his Son to make sons, and puts his Son's own cry for the Father into orphaned mouths.

In the early centuries the church fought to say that the Son was of the very same substance as the Father—*homoousios*, the word hammered out at Nicaea in 325—and it mattered enormously for exactly this. If the Son who cried *Abba* is truly God, then when his Spirit puts that same cry in your mouth, you are not addressing a distant deity through a hired intermediary. You are speaking to God with the Son's own word, from inside the family, as one whom God himself has placed as a son. The doctrine the church bled over in the fourth century is the reason the word *Abba* in your mouth is not presumption. It is your birthright.

And here is where it lands, and where it must land, in mercy. You cannot be un-adopted. A slave can be sold; a son cannot be un-sonned. "So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God" (Galatians 4:7). The inheritance is not held out ahead of you as a wage to be earned. It is already yours, because you are already his. The Spirit crying *Abba* in your chest this morning is not the beginning of your effort to become a son. It is God's own guarantee that you already are.

- **A. A son does not audition for his place at the table.** — The heir is not on trial. He belongs by birth—by new birth, by the sending of the Son and the sending of the Spirit—and no amount of failure demotes him to servant, and no amount of performance was ever what got him in. Stop auditioning for a role you already have.
- **B. The Spirit's cry is the proof you cannot manufacture.** — You did not work up the word *Abba*. It was placed in you. That cry is not your achievement handed up to God; it is God's own gift handed down, the evidence in your own mouth that the adoption is finished. When you cry Father, you are not asking to be let in. You are speaking from inside.

A son does not earn his inheritance.

## Free, and Walking by the Spirit: Freedom That Is Not License (Galatians 5:1-26)
*Christ set us free for freedom, and that freedom is not room to indulge the flesh but room to walk by the Spirit*

**Text:** Galatians 5:1-26 · **Supporting:** John 8:36 · Romans 8:4 · Romans 6:1-2 · 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 · Leviticus 19:18 · Romans 13:10

There are two ways to lose your freedom, and Paul has been fighting one of them for four chapters. The first is to go back under the law, to trade grace for a scoreboard. But there is a second, and Paul turns to it now, because the moment you tell people they are free, some of them hear permission to do whatever the flesh wants. Freedom from the law, they think, means freedom to sin. Paul says no—and he says it with a phrase that carries the whole chapter. "For freedom Christ has set us free" (Galatians 5:1). Free *for* something. Not free *from* everything. Freedom with a direction.

We flatten freedom into the absence of constraint. To us, free means no one tells me what to do. But Paul's freedom is not a vacuum. It is a liberation from two masters at once—the law that condemns and the flesh that enslaves—into the service of a third thing that is not slavery at all. The Christian is not set loose to do as he pleases. He is set free to become what love looks like, and that turns out to be the only freedom worth the name.

### I. Do Not Submit Again to a Yoke of Slavery (Galatians 5:1-15)

Paul begins with the exit from the law, and the language is a released prisoner's. "Stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1). The false teachers were selling circumcision as an upgrade; Paul calls it a yoke, the wooden beam laid across an ox. And he issues a warning that admits no middle ground. "I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law. You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace" (Galatians 5:3-4). *Severed.* Take on the law as your ground of acceptance and you have unhooked yourself from Christ, because the two cannot both be the ground. You stand on grace or you stand on your own record. There is no both.

Then the sentence that resolves the whole tension of the letter into one economy. "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love" (Galatians 5:6). *Faith working through love.* Not faith versus works, as if the Christian did nothing. Faith that goes to work—and the work it does is love. This is Paul's answer to everyone who thinks grace makes us lazy. Grace does not produce idleness. It produces a faith that cannot sit still, and the direction it moves is toward the neighbor.

- **A. Falling from grace is not sinning too much—it is trusting your own record.** — We use the phrase "fallen from grace" for a person who has failed morally. Paul uses it for a person who has succeeded religiously and now trusts that success. To fall from grace is not to sin your way out; it is to perform your way out, to make your law-keeping the thing you stand on. The moralist is in more danger here than the failure.
- **B. The whole law is fulfilled in one word—love.** — "For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself'" (Galatians 5:14, quoting Leviticus 19:18). Freedom from the law does not mean the law's aim is abandoned. Its aim—love—is finally reached, not by gritted-teeth compliance, but by a freed heart. The law could command love and never produce it. The Spirit produces what the law could only demand.

### II. Walk by the Spirit, and Bear His Fruit (Galatians 5:16-26)

Then the second danger, and Paul names it head-on. "For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another" (Galatians 5:13). *Opportunity*—the Greek is *aphormē*, a base of operations, a launching point. The flesh will treat your freedom as a beachhead. Paul's answer is not to reinstate the law but to name the power that actually defeats the flesh. "But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh" (Galatians 5:16).

Watch the mechanism. Paul does not say: try harder not to sin. He says: walk by the Spirit, and the not-sinning follows. The flesh is not overcome by white-knuckled restraint but by a competing and stronger desire. "For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do" (Galatians 5:17). There is a war inside the believer, and you do not win it by managing behavior. You win it by which one you walk with.

Then the two harvests. The works of the flesh Paul lists as a scattered mess—"sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry... enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger" (Galatians 5:19-20)—the disintegration of a life. And against it, one thing, singular. "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control" (Galatians 5:22-23). Not fruits, plural, as if you could select a few. Fruit, singular—one cluster, growing together, the single character of a Spirit-walked life. And *fruit* is the exact right word, because you do not manufacture fruit. You do not strain to produce it. A branch bears it by staying connected to the vine. The Spirit-life is grown, not built.

- **A. The flesh is defeated by a stronger desire, not by sheer restraint.** — "Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh." The order matters. Behavior modification without the Spirit is just the law wearing a Christian mask, and it fails the same way the law failed. You do not starve the flesh into submission. You outgrow it by walking with something better.
- **B. Fruit is grown, not manufactured.** — Love, joy, peace—these are not tasks on a checklist. They are what grows in a life connected to the Spirit, the way apples grow on a tree that no one commanded to try harder. "Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires" (Galatians 5:24). The old self is not being managed. It has been nailed up, and something new is growing in its place.

### III. The Freedom We Keep Turning Back Into a Cage

I have taken the two exits Paul warns against, sometimes in the same week. I have used grace as a permission slip, told myself the cross covers it, and indulged the flesh under the banner of Christian freedom. And I have swung the other way, rebuilt the yoke, tried to sanctify myself by anxiety and rule-keeping until my faith had no love in it at all—just compliance and fear. Both are slavery. I have preached freedom and lived in one cage or the other, and I built both cages myself.

We do this because real freedom is terrifying. License is a cage that feels like liberty—do whatever you want, and be quietly owned by your appetites. Legalism is a cage that feels like safety—keep the rules, and never risk the vulnerability of grace. Both let us stay in control. Walking by the Spirit is the one path that takes control out of our hands, because you cannot schedule fruit, you can only stay connected and wait. And something in us would rather run our own cage than be free on someone else's terms.

Our own culture has bet its whole identity on the license cage and called it freedom. Freedom, it says, is the absence of anyone telling you what to do—no authority, no constraint, no master. And it has produced a generation freer than any in history and more owned by its appetites than any in memory, medicated, anxious, enslaved to the very desires it was told would liberate it. Paul saw the con two thousand years early. Freedom is not the absence of a master. It is the presence of the right one. The unbeliever indulging every desire and the legalist crushing every desire are both missing the only door out, which is not less desire or more restraint, but a stronger and better love.

Augustine, in his *Confessions* in the year 397, wrote the line the whole Christian tradition has never gotten past: our hearts are restless until they rest in God. He had chased freedom through every appetite the flesh could name and found each one a new master. He discovered what Paul is preaching here—that the will set loose from God is not free but enslaved to its own cravings, and that true freedom is not the absence of a master but the presence of the right one. "So love God," Augustine wrote in the same era, "and do what you will"—not because anything goes, but because a heart truly walking with the Spirit will want the things love wants. That is Galatians 5 in a sentence sixteen centuries old.

And here is the mercy that keeps this from becoming one more law. The freedom does not depend on how well you walk. Christ set you free—past tense, finished, "for freedom Christ has set us free." Your walking by the Spirit is not the price of your freedom; it is the fruit of it. On the days you stumble into one cage or the other, the answer is not to earn your way back but to remember you were never freed on the basis of your walking in the first place. The one who "loved me and gave himself for me" set me free, and he did not do it so I could return to slavery. He did it so that, connected to him, I might finally become what love looks like.

- **A. License and legalism are the same slavery wearing different clothes.** — One indulges the flesh and one polishes it, but both keep you in control and both keep you from the Spirit. The freed man is not the one who does whatever he wants, nor the one who keeps every rule in fear. He is the one who walks by the Spirit and finds, growing in him, the love he could never command.
- **B. Freedom is for serving, not for self.** — "Through love serve one another" (Galatians 5:13). The whole point of being set free from the scoreboard is that you no longer have to spend your life earning your own standing—so your life is finally free to be spent on someone else. Freedom that curves back on the self is just a nicer name for slavery. Freedom that pours out in love is the only kind Christ died to give.

Freedom serves through love, not self.

## Bearing Burdens, Boasting Only in the Cross (Galatians 6:1-18)
*Those who live by the Spirit carry each other, and at the end there is only one thing left worth boasting in*

**Text:** Galatians 6:1-18 · **Supporting:** Romans 15:1 · 1 Corinthians 3:8 · 2 Corinthians 9:6 · Philippians 3:3 · Matthew 11:30 · Romans 12:15

Paul spends five chapters tearing down a false gospel, and then, at the end, he shows you what the true one looks like on a Tuesday morning. Not in the abstract. In how you treat the man in your church who just fell. The gospel of grace, worked all the way down into a congregation, produces a particular kind of person—one who bends down toward the failure of another instead of stepping over it. Everything Paul has argued about justification comes to ground here, in a room where somebody sinned and everybody else has to decide what kind of people grace has made them.

And then he ends the letter the way he began it—hot, personal, taking the pen into his own hand—and he draws a line under everything with a single word. *Boast.* Every human being boasts in something, stakes their worth on something, holds something up as the thing that makes them count. The Judaizers boasted in circumcision, in the flesh they could display. Paul says he has exactly one thing left to hold up, and it is the most shameful object the ancient world knew.

### I. Carry One Another's Burdens (Galatians 6:1-10)

Paul begins with the fallen brother, and the tone is a surgeon's, careful and tender. "Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted" (Galatians 6:1). *Restore*—the word is *katartizō*, used for setting a broken bone or mending a net. The goal is not exposure. It is repair. And the same breath that tells you to restore the sinner tells you to watch yourself, because the distance between the one who fell and the one doing the restoring is thinner than the restorer thinks.

Then the sentence that names the shape of a gospel community. "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2). *Fulfill the law of Christ*—the law that could not justify anyone is fulfilled, at last, not by keeping rules but by carrying weight for each other. This is the freedom of chapter 5 in action. Set free from earning your own standing, you now have your hands empty enough to pick up someone else's load. And Paul is careful to distinguish this from a paralyzing self-neglect: "For each will have to bear his own load" (Galatians 6:5). There is a burden too heavy to carry alone that others must help lift, and there is a personal responsibility no one can carry for you. The gospel gives you both a community and a spine.

Under it all runs a law as fixed as gravity. "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap. For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life" (Galatians 6:7-8). This is the whole letter in an agricultural image. The flesh and the Spirit are two fields, and you are planting in one of them every day. There is no neutral ground and no crop that comes up different from the seed. "And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up" (Galatians 6:9).

- **A. Restoration, not exposure, is the mark of Spirit-people.** — When a brother falls, the flesh wants distance and a verdict; the Spirit wants a mended bone. The church that grace has actually reached does not step over its wounded or put them on display. It kneels down beside them "in a spirit of gentleness," and it does so with one eye on its own capacity to fall.
- **B. You are always sowing—there is no fallow year.** — Every day is seed going into one field or the other, and the harvest is not arbitrary. This is not the law returning as a threat; it is the Spirit's realism about a life. Grace does not suspend sowing and reaping. It changes which field you plant in.

### II. Boasting Only in the Cross (Galatians 6:11-18)

Then Paul takes the pen. "See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand" (Galatians 6:11)—he grabs it from the scribe to sign off in person, and what he writes is a final exposure of his opponents' real motive. "It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised, and only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ" (Galatians 6:12). There it is. The whole false gospel came down to fear and image. They wanted a religion they could display and a discipleship that cost them nothing. Circumcision was a way to look devout and dodge the offense of the cross. "That they may boast in your flesh" (Galatians 6:13)—your compliance was going to be their trophy.

And against the trophy religion, Paul plants his flag on the one object the ancient world used to break men. "But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world" (Galatians 6:14). The cross. A Roman execution device, a symbol of humiliation so total that Cicero said the very word should be kept far from the ears of a Roman citizen. Paul says: that is my only boast. Not my heritage, not my discipline, not my record. A gallows. The place where the God I could not earn my way to gave himself for me.

And the cross does something in both directions. "The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world." The old economy of showing off in the flesh, of earning standing, of boasting in performance—Paul is dead to it, and it is dead to him. That is why he can end on the sentence that undoes every distinction the false teachers lived by. "For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation" (Galatians 6:15). *Kainē ktisis.* A new creation. Not a reformed old self, not a better-behaved flesh—a new making, the beginning of the world God is remaking through the cross.

- **A. The false gospel is always about looking good and avoiding cost.** — Paul strips his opponents down to two motives: they wanted to make a showing, and they wanted to skip the persecution the cross brings. Every performance religion runs on the same two engines—the desire to be seen as devout, and the refusal to bear the offense of a crucified God. Grace has no room for either.
- **B. The cross crucifies the whole scoreboard.** — When Paul boasts only in the cross, the entire system of comparison dies—both his standing over the world and the world's hold over him. A man boasting in the cross has nothing left to prove and nothing left to protect, because the thing he boasts in is the death of his own performing self.

### III. What We Actually Boast In

I know the trophy religion from the inside, because I have practiced it. I have wanted to make a good showing—wanted the church to grow so I would look like a pastor who had it figured out, wanted my discipline and my doctrine to be the thing people admired. That is boasting in the flesh with a Bible in my hand. And I have quietly preferred the versions of discipleship that would not get me mocked, trimmed the offense off the cross so the message would go down easier and cost me less. The men Paul is exposing are not strangers. I have been them, from a pulpit, with large letters in my own hand.

We are all boasting in something, every one of us, all the time. We just hide it better than the Judaizers did. We boast in our theology being more correct than the church down the road. We boast in our family looking whole, our morality holding up, our tribe being the right one. We boast in our very humility, in how little we boast. The flesh has infinite trophies, and it will happily let you build your identity on any of them—including your Christianity—as long as the thing you finally hold up is you.

In the second century, a man named Polycarp, an old bishop who had known the apostle John, was arrested and told to renounce Christ or die. He said he had served Christ eighty-six years and would not deny the King who had saved him, and he was burned. He had exactly one thing to boast in, and it was not his record or his reputation or his flesh—it was the crucified and risen Lord who had loved him, and he would not trade it to save his own life. That is a man to whom the world had been crucified. That is what it looks like when the cross, and not the self, becomes the only trophy left in a person's hands.

And here is where the whole letter comes to rest, and it rests, finally, in mercy. If your only boast is the cross, then you have nothing to protect and nothing to prove, and that is the most freeing place a human being can stand. You cannot be humiliated out of a standing you never earned. You cannot be exposed as a fraud when your entire hope was another man's righteousness from the start. "Peace and mercy be upon all who walk by this rule, even upon the Israel of God" (Galatians 6:16). The rule is the cross. The peace comes when you finally stop boasting in yourself and let the crucified Christ be the only thing you hold up—because he is the only thing that will still be standing when everything you might have boasted in is gone.

- **A. Everyone boasts—the only question is in what.** — The issue was never whether you would build your identity on something; you cannot help it. The issue is whether the thing you hold up is the flesh, which will fail you, or the cross, which already held when you could not. The false gospel just gives you a religious flesh to boast in. The true one takes even that away.
- **B. The cross leaves you nothing to protect and nothing to prove.** — A man whose only boast is a Roman gallows has already lost the game the world is playing, and in losing it he is free. There is no reputation left to guard, no record left to defend, no showing left to make. What remains is grace, and a new creation, and the marks of Jesus, which Paul says he bears on his body. Boast in that, or you will spend your life boasting in something that is already dying.

Boast in the cross or boast in nothing.
